stem: For a normal distribution with mean 50 and standard deviation 10, what is the value of the median?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Subtracting one standard deviation (50 - 10 = 40) confuses mean with some other location measure.
For any normal distribution, mean = median = mode because the distribution is perfectly symmetric about its centre.
Adding one standard deviation (50 + 10 = 60) mistakes the median for a quantile above the mean.
Taking half of 10 and subtracting (50 - 5 = 45) is a computational error with no conceptual basis.

explanation: In a normal distribution the three measures of central tendency coincide: mean = median = mode = mu. The perfect left-right symmetry about mu guarantees exactly half the area lies on each side, making mu the median by definition.

explanation_sections.punchline: Normal symmetry forces mean = median = mode, so the median equals the given mean of 50.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify the distribution property: for a normal distribution, the probability density function is symmetric about mu, which means the cumulative distribution function equals 0.5 exactly at mu. By definition the median is the point where CDF = 0.5, so median = mu = 50.
explanation_sections.lesson: For any normal distribution, all three central tendency measures equal mu; changing variance never shifts this.
explanation_sections.timing: Recall-only, under 20 seconds. Eliminate options that add or subtract any multiple of sigma from mu.
